State forest lands are arranged into blocks called Compartments. A compartment may be a contiguous area of state-owned lands or a compilation of nearby non-contiguous areas within in a Forest Management Unit (FMU), State Park, State Game Area or other designation. Compartments provide a convenient location reference, a metric for distributing management activities over time, and a discrete unit for planning purposes. Compartments range in size from less than 100 acres to over 5,000 acres with a typical size of about 1,500 to 3,000 acres. Smaller compartments are necessary in areas of fragmented ownership or used when management objectives are more readily met. Larger compartments may be used to improve operational efficiencies, when management objectives require large areas for specific goals, or to include an entire unit in the same compartment (e.g., a large State Park or State Game Areas). Compartment boundaries are usually static except in the case of minor adjustment of stand lines sharing a compartment boundary or if a case is made to change boundaries to align with management goals. For forest management activities specifically, compartments were developed to: Summarize data and make treatment recommendations on an area small enough to allow quick visualization of existing conditions and the effects of treatments. Systematically examine and consider treatments in a localized forest acreage. Disperse treatments spatially across the FMU. Disperse treatments temporally across the FMU as each compartment is also assigned one of ten Years of Entry. Attempt to ensure even distribution of treatment acres across years. DNR Managed Sites<\/strong> <\/span>is a comprehensive, statewide geospatial dataset representing physical locations of assets and sites administered or maintained by the Michigan Department of Natural Resources (DNR). Each point feature corresponds to an on-the-ground facility, operational site, recreation feature, or management location that plays a role in delivering DNR programs and services across the state.<\/span><\/p>

This dataset consolidates information from multiple DNR divisions and program areas into a single, standardized asset inventory. It serves as an authoritative reference layer for public transparency, internal planning, maintenance scheduling, recreational access mapping, and cross\u2011divisional coordination.<\/span><\/p>

What the Layer Represents<\/strong><\/span><\/h2>

The features in this layer represent a wide variety of asset types\u2014from parks and recreation sites to fisheries facilities, wildlife management areas, forest management units, harbors, public access sites, and more. Each record includes standardized classification fields that identify:<\/span><\/p>

  • the type of asset (e.g., building, access point, site)<\/span><\/li>
  • a refined detail type for further categorization<\/span><\/li>
  • ownership authority (e.g., DNR division, State, Federal, County, Tribal, or private partner)<\/span><\/li>
  • the specific DNR management unit responsible for administration or maintenance<\/span><\/li>
  • the functional purpose of the site (e.g., Recreation, Forestry, Wildlife, Access, Water, Utility)<\/span><\/li><\/ul>

    These attributes enable users to explore assets by program area, management responsibility, asset purpose, and physical characteristics.<\/span><\/p>

    Rich Attribute Structure for Asset Management<\/strong><\/span><\/h2>

    The layer includes coded value domains for several fields to ensure consistent terminology across DNR programs. Condition ratings enable standardized assessments for planning and maintenance workflows. Functional classifications support program reporting and resource allocation. Surface material categories provide insights into recreation infrastructure and trail/site composition.<\/span><\/p>

    Additional metadata fields record:<\/span><\/p>

    • the method by which each asset was mapped or collected (survey\u2011grade, GNSS, aerial imagery, etc.)<\/span><\/li>
    • the type of edit activity applied during lifecycle management<\/span><\/li>
    • GNSS-derived latitude and longitude<\/span><\/li>
    • automatic editor tracking fields for accountability and version history<\/span><\/li><\/ul>

      This detailed schema supports data reliability and completeness across all DNR asset types.<\/span><\/p>

      Data Collection and Quality<\/strong><\/span><\/h2>

      Records may originate from field inventories, GNSS collection, program-level databases, aerial image interpretation, or historic systems. The Collect Type<\/strong> field indicates the positional accuracy and method used to acquire the spatial location, ranging from high\u2011precision survey data to field-observed or legacy records. The Edit Type<\/strong> field describes how the record has evolved, capturing additions, updates, repositioning, splits, or proposed assets.<\/span><\/p>

      Integration and Cross\u2011Divisional Use<\/strong><\/span><\/h2>

      Because the dataset harmonizes assets from divisions including PRD, WLD, FOD, FRD, Fisheries, Law Enforcement, and the Office of Minerals Management, it acts as a central reference dataset for enterprise-wide DNR mapping. It can be integrated into:<\/span><\/p>

      • public-facing web viewers and recreation maps<\/span><\/li>
      • internal dashboards for park operations, wildlife management, and forestry planning<\/span><\/li>
      • field mobility applications for maintenance crews and site inspection workflows<\/span><\/li>
      • cross\u2011agency coordination, emergency response planning, and resource conservation initiatives<\/span><\/li><\/ul>

        Its consistent schema enables complex spatial queries, thematic mapping, and aggregation of asset information across divisions or geographic service areas.<\/span><\/p>

        Intended Audience and Applications<\/strong><\/span><\/h2>

        The dataset is used by:<\/p>

        • DNR staff for operations, planning, and inventory management<\/span><\/li>
        • Researchers and conservation planners<\/span><\/li>
        • Local governments and partner organizations<\/span><\/li>
        • Members of the public seeking recreation or site information<\/span><\/li>
        • GIS professionals looking for authoritative state-managed asset data<\/span><\/li><\/ul>

          Update Frequency<\/strong><\/span><\/h2>

          The data is actively maintained by DNR GIS staff and division program leads. Editor tracking fields provide timestamps and user information for every change, supporting transparent data stewardship and real-time accuracy improvement.<\/span><\/p>

          Contact Information<\/strong><\/span><\/p>
